description: Periodic table arrangement, Group 1 alkali metals, Group 7 halogens, and Group 0 noble gases.
content_html:
The Development of the Periodic Table

In the nineteenth century, scientists searched for a way to organise the growing number of known elements. Dmitri Mendeleev produced the most successful early arrangement around 1869. He ordered elements by atomic weight but made two crucial decisions that others had not: he left deliberate gaps for elements that had not yet been discovered, and he swapped the order of a few elements so that those with similar chemical properties lined up in the same vertical columns. When subsequently discovered elements — including gallium and germanium — matched the properties he had predicted for the gaps, his table gained wide acceptance. The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of atomic number (proton number) rather than atomic weight, which resolved the few anomalies in Mendeleev’s arrangement.

Key Fact

Elements in the periodic table are arranged in order of atomic number. Elements in the same group (column) have the same number of outer electrons and similar chemical properties. Elements in the same period (row) have the same number of electron shells. Metals are on the left and centre; non-metals are on the right.

Group 1 — The Alkali Metals

The alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium) all have one electron in their outer shell. They are soft, low-density metals with relatively low melting points compared to most metals. All react vigorously with water, producing a metal hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas. The general equation for the reaction with water is:

$$\text{metal} + H_2O \rightarrow \text{metal hydroxide} + H_2$$

For example, sodium reacts with water according to:

$$2Na(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + H_2(g)$$

Going down Group 1, reactivity increases. This is because the outer electron is in a shell that is increasingly far from the nucleus, and so is more weakly attracted by the positive nuclear charge. The outer electron is therefore more easily lost. Potassium reacts faster and more vigorously with water than sodium, which in turn reacts faster than lithium. Melting points decrease and densities generally increase going down the group.

Flame tests allow you to identify metal ions by the colour they produce when heated in a Bunsen flame. A clean platinum or nichrome wire loop is dipped into the sample and held in the hottest part of the flame. Group 1 metal flame colours: lithium → crimson, sodium → yellow, potassium → lilac. This is a practical activity group (PAG C4) context — you should be able to describe the method, identify metals from flame colours, and explain why each loop must be cleaned between tests (to avoid contamination from previous samples).

Group 7 — The Halogens

The halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine) have seven electrons in their outer shell and exist as diatomic molecules (\(F_2\), \(Cl_2\), \(Br_2\), \(I_2\)). They need to gain just one electron to achieve a full outer shell, which makes them very reactive non-metals. At room temperature, chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid, and iodine is a dark grey solid. Going down Group 7, the boiling point increases as the molecules get larger.

Going down Group 7, reactivity decreases. This is because the outer shell is further from the nucleus in atoms lower in the group, making it harder for the nucleus to attract an extra electron. A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt. For example, chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide solution:

$$Cl_2(aq) + 2KBr(aq) \rightarrow 2KCl(aq) + Br_2(aq)$$

If chlorine is added to potassium iodide solution, a brown colour develops as iodine is displaced. If bromine is added to potassium chloride solution, no reaction occurs because bromine is less reactive than chlorine.

Key Fact

Group 1: reactivity increases going down (outer electron lost more easily as it is further from the nucleus). Group 7: reactivity decreases going down (harder to gain an electron as the outer shell is further from the nucleus). These trends are opposite because metals lose electrons while non-metals gain them.

Group 0 — The Noble Gases

The noble gases (helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon) have completely full outer electron shells. This makes them very stable and extremely unreactive — they do not normally form compounds. They exist as single atoms (monatomic) rather than as molecules. Their boiling points increase going down the group as the atoms get larger and intermolecular forces increase. Noble gases have many practical applications: helium in weather balloons and airships (less dense than air, non-flammable), neon in display lighting (glows a distinctive red-orange), and argon in tungsten filament light bulbs and in welding (inert atmosphere prevents oxidation).

An element’s position in the periodic table lets you predict its reactions. Group number tells you how many outer electrons the atom has, which tells you how it bonds. Period number tells you how many electron shells it has, and going down a group the outer shell moves further from the nucleus. Mendeleev used exactly this logic to predict the properties of undiscovered elements — he predicted the density, melting point and typical compounds of elements such as gallium before they were discovered. The predictions were confirmed when the elements were isolated, which powerfully validated the periodic table as a predictive tool, not just a classification system.
exam_tip_html: In explain questions about group trends, always state the direction of the trend first, then give the electron-level reason. For Group 1 reactivity: “Reactivity increases going down because the outer electron is further from the nucleus, is less strongly attracted, and so is more easily lost.” For Group 7 reactivity: “Reactivity decreases because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, making it harder for the atom to attract and gain an extra electron.” A common error in displacement questions is to give the wrong equation or to add the wrong halogen. Always check: the more reactive halogen displaces the less reactive one, not the other way round.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Elements are arranged by atomic number. Groups share the same outer electron count and similar properties; periods share the same number of electron shells. Mendeleev’s key contributions were leaving gaps and predicting the properties of undiscovered elements.
  • Group 1 reactivity increases down the group (outer electron lost more easily); Group 7 reactivity decreases down the group (harder to gain an electron further from the nucleus). More reactive halogens displace less reactive ones from their salts.
  • Group 0 noble gases are unreactive because they have full outer electron shells. Flame tests identify Group 1 metals: lithium (crimson), sodium (yellow), potassium (lilac).

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a property of all Group 1 elements?
A) They are non-metals
B) They have two electrons in their outer shell
C) They react with water to produce hydrogen gas
D) Their reactivity decreases going down the group
practice_questions.marks: C) They react with water to produce hydrogen gas [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the flame test colour for sodium and for potassium.
practice_questions.marks: Sodium: yellow (or orange-yellow). Potassium: lilac (or violet). Both required for the mark. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what you would observe when chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes visible colour change (solution turns orange or brown) AND identifies that bromine has been displaced/formed.
Secure: Identifies colour change and states bromine is produced.
Developing: States a colour change but does not explain which substance caused it.
Emerging: States “a reaction occurs” without describing what is observed.

practice_questions.text: Explain why potassium is more reactive with water than lithium.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Potassium’s outer electron is in a higher energy level, further from the nucleus. There is more electron shielding from inner shells. The electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is weaker. Therefore the outer electron is lost more easily, making potassium more reactive.
Secure: Outer electron further from nucleus, less strongly held, more easily lost.
Developing: States outer electron is further away but does not link to ease of losing it.
Emerging: Just states “potassium is lower in the group” without an explanation.

practice_questions.text: Bromine has atomic number 35 and exists as Br2 molecules. Predict whether bromine will react with potassium iodide solution. Write a balanced symbol equation for any reaction that occurs and explain your reasoning.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly predicts that bromine will react (more reactive than iodine) [1]. Balanced equation: Br2(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KBr(aq) + I2(aq) [1]. Explains bromine is more reactive because its outer shell is closer to the nucleus, making it easier to gain an electron [1]. States this is a displacement reaction [1].
Secure: Correct prediction with balanced equation and a linked explanation.
Developing: Correct prediction and equation but explanation is incomplete.
Emerging: Correct prediction but equation unbalanced and little explanation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how well Mendeleev’s early periodic table predicted the existence and properties of undiscovered elements. Refer to specific examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Discusses Mendeleev leaving gaps; explains he predicted density, melting point and compounds for missing elements; gives example(s) such as gallium or germanium; evaluates that subsequent discoveries confirmed his predictions, validating the table as a predictive tool not just a classification. Considers limitations (e.g. occasional need to swap elements, later refined by atomic number).
Secure: Explains gaps and predictions, names at least one element, links discovery to validation.
Developing: Explains gaps but examples are vague; limited evaluation.
Emerging: Describes Mendeleev’s table in general terms without specifics.

knowledge_checks.q: What does the group number in the periodic table tell you about an element?
options: The number of protons in the nucleus
The number of electrons in the outer shell

flashcard_questions.q: What did Mendeleev leave in his periodic table for undiscovered elements?
flashcard_questions.a: Gaps, with predicted properties for the missing elements.

flashcard_questions.q: Modern periodic table: in what order are elements arranged?
flashcard_questions.a: In order of atomic number (proton number).

flashcard_questions.q: What does the period number tell you about an element's atoms?
flashcard_questions.a: The number of electron shells they have.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do Group 1 elements react with water?
flashcard_questions.a: They have one outer electron that is easily lost, forming metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the answer to: Flame test colour for lithium?
What is the answer to: Flame test colour for potassium?
Why does Group 1 reactivity increase going down the group?
flashcard_questions.a: The outer electron is further from the nucleus, held less strongly, and is more easily lost.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Group 7 reactivity decrease going down the group?
flashcard_questions.a: The outer shell is further from the nucleus, making it harder to attract and gain an extra electron.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a halogen displacement reaction?
flashcard_questions.a: A more reactive halogen replaces a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are noble gases very unreactive?
flashcard_questions.a: They have completely full outer electron shells, making them very stable.

flashcard_questions.q: At room temperature: state of chlorine, bromine and iodine.
flashcard_questions.a: Chlorine is a gas, bromine is a liquid, iodine is a solid.

glossary_terms.definition: The Russian chemist who arranged elements by atomic weight, left gaps for undiscovered elements, and predicted their properties — creating the first widely accepted periodic table around 1869.
The elements in Group 1 of the periodic table (lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium, francium). They have one outer electron and are very reactive metals.
The elements in Group 7 of the periodic table (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine). They have seven outer electrons and exist as diatomic molecules.
A molecule made of exactly two atoms of the same element bonded together, such as Cl2, Br2 or I2.
A reaction where a more reactive halogen replaces a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt.
The unreactive elements in Group 0 of the periodic table (helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon). They have full outer electron shells, making them very stable.
